name: New Bedford
headline: Cobblestones above the working harbor,
and the train back on Acushnet Avenue.
answer: New Bedford is a Bristol County city of 101,079 people (2020 Census) on the Acushnet River where it meets Buzzards Bay. Its downtown waterfront is part of New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park, established in 1996. The Warren Group counted 401 single-family sales in 2025. Since March 24, 2025, the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line has run from New Bedford and Church Street stations to Boston's South Station, and I-195 crosses the city.
overview: New Bedford was incorporated as a town in 1787 and became a city in 1847. In the first half of the 1800s it was one of the world's most important whaling ports, and in 1857 its harbor counted 329 vessels. The downtown historic district, 11 city blocks and part of a twelfth west of the waterfront, keeps Federal and Greek Revival buildings put up mostly between 1790 and 1855, including Seamen's Bethel and the 1836 U.S. Customhouse. Frederick Douglass settled in the city in 1838 and lived there until 1841.

When whaling faded, cotton mills took over, and the Wamsutta Mills were for a time the world's largest weaving plant. The housing that followed spreads out from downtown: the County Street Historic District, laid out in the 18th century, holds City Hall, the library and large houses in Greek Revival and Gothic Revival styles, while Acushnet Heights keeps wood-frame houses built for factory workers from the 1860s on. Buttonwood Park and its zoo sit to the west, and Fort Taber Park occupies Clark's Point, the city's southern tip on Buzzards Bay.

The 2020 Census counted 44,588 housing units in New Bedford, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 survey puts the owner-occupied share at 40.3 percent. In March 2023 the city published Building New Bedford, a housing plan that set a 90-day approval target for large multifamily projects, proposed smaller minimum lots and lower parking minimums (then two spaces per new unit), and called for allowing detached accessory dwellings, which were then prohibited. As a commuter rail community under the MBTA Communities law, the city needed multifamily zoning near its new stations: the City Council approved a transit-oriented district along Kings Highway, around Church Street station in the North End, in November 2024, and the state lists New Bedford as compliant as of October 21, 2026. A second overlay, the Clasky Common district along Purchase Street near New Bedford station, was proposed in early 2025.

housing.text: The 2020 Census counted 44,588 housing units in New Bedford, and the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 American Community Survey puts the owner-occupied share at 40.3 percent. The city's 2023 Building New Bedford plan counted 39,059 occupied units, 60.2 percent of them rented, and noted that triple-deckers are abundant and that surrounding towns have a higher share of single-family homes. Older neighborhoods mix 19th-century wood-frame houses with downtown commercial and mixed-use blocks, and The Warren Group recorded 401 single-family sales in 2025.

villages.name: Downtown and the Waterfront
villages.line: The historic district between Front, Elm and Commercial Streets and Acushnet Avenue, about 11 city blocks of Federal and Greek Revival buildings beside the harbor.

villages.name: County Street
villages.line: About 100 acres along County Street, roughly bounded by Acushnet, Page, Middle and Bedford Streets, with City Hall, the library and Greek Revival, Gothic Revival and Late Victorian buildings.

villages.name: Acushnet Heights
villages.line: About 20 acres around Clasky Common Park, bounded by Purchase, Linden and County Streets, with wood-frame houses built from the 1860s for factory workers and four 19th-century churches.

villages.name: Clark's Point
villages.line: The southernmost point of the city, where the Acushnet River meets Buzzards Bay, home to Fort Taber Park.

villages.name: Central New Bedford
villages.line: A 29-acre rectangle bounded by Acushnet Avenue and School, Middle and Sixth Streets, with 79 buildings, mostly commercial or mixed-use and built up in the late 19th century, including the 1908-10 Registry of Deeds and the 1915 Post Office.

villages.name: Howland Mill Village
villages.line: A 9.9-acre district roughly bounded by Bolton, Winsper and Hemlock Streets and Rockdale Avenue, with single-family cottages built in 1888-89 for the nearby Howland Mill on just two floor plans, and double-decker houses added in the 1920s.

rail.line: Fall River/New Bedford Line (New Bedford branch)

commute.text: Commuter rail returned on March 24, 2025, after a gap since 1958. New Bedford and Church Street stations sit on the New Bedford branch of the Fall River/New Bedford Line, which runs through East Taunton, Middleborough, Brockton and Quincy to Boston's South Station; sample outbound weekday trips on the current timetable take about 1 hour 40 to 45 minutes, and the timetable also shows weekend trains to New Bedford. Both stations are in fare zone 8 and have full high-level platforms; New Bedford station shares the Whale's Tooth lot with the SeaStreak ferry and has 150 spaces for rail riders, and Church Street station, in the North End off Church Street, has 355. I-195 crosses the city toward Providence and Wareham, Route 18 links it to the waterfront, and Route 140 runs north to Route 24 in Taunton. SRTA runs local buses, and SeaStreak ferries sail from New Bedford to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, with separate service to Cuttyhunk Island.

places.name: New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park
places.line: A fee-free national park in downtown New Bedford, with its visitor center at 33 William Street.

places.name: New Bedford Whaling Museum
places.line: Founded in 1903 by the Old Dartmouth Historical Society, at 18 Johnny Cake Hill.

places.name: Buttonwood Park Zoo
places.line: A city-owned, AZA-accredited zoo at 425 Hawthorn Street, with animals from five continents.

places.name: Fort Taber Park
places.line: A 47-acre park at Clark's Point with the 1857 stone fort, Endicott-era batteries and the Fort Taber/Fort Rodman military museum.

places.name: Seamen's Bethel
places.line: A white clapboard chapel in the downtown historic district, first built in 1832 and rebuilt after an 1867 fire.

history.text: Incorporated as a town on February 23; it became a city on March 18, 1847.
Frederick Douglass settled in New Bedford, where he lived and worked on the wharves until 1841.
The waterfront historic district was designated a National Historic Landmark on November 13.
Commuter rail service to Boston resumed on March 24, the first since 1958.

search_notes: 'New Bedford MA real estate agent' returns directory and profile pages (BiggerPockets, HomeLight, Ramsey Solutions, Experience.com, RealTrends, Century 21), including HomeLight pages for the Clifford and Rockdale areas. 'Moving to New Bedford MA' is almost all movers (Lugg, MoveBuddha, LocalMovers, American Van Lines) plus Livability. No ranking result explains the new commuter rail stations, the historic districts or the national park, which a sourced guide could cover.

faq.q: What is the median home price in New Bedford, MA?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, the median single-family sale price in New Bedford for calendar year 2025 was $422,000, across 401 sales. In 2024 it was $395,000, across 412 sales.

faq.q: Does New Bedford have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes. Since March 24, 2025, New Bedford station (536 Acushnet Avenue) and Church Street station (387 Church Street) have been served by the MBTA Fall River/New Bedford Line to Boston's South Station. The current timetable shows trains to New Bedford on weekdays and weekends.

faq.q: Is there a ferry from New Bedford?
faq.a: Yes. SeaStreak runs ferries from New Bedford to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, and the Cuttyhunk Ferry Company runs scheduled service to Cuttyhunk Island. Check the operators for seasonal schedules.

faq.q: Which school district serves New Bedford?
faq.a: New Bedford Public Schools. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in New Bedford, MA?
faq.a: According to the Massachusetts Division of Local Services, New Bedford's FY2026 residential property tax rate is $10.95 per $1,000 of assessed value, and commercial, industrial and personal property pay $21.80. No residential exemption is noted in the sources used for this guide; the Assessors' Office handles personal exemptions, such as those for seniors and veterans.
